text:
CITATION
:

N.H.B. v. L.B., 2012 ONSC
1454

COURT
FILE NO.:
CV-08-00359385-0000

MOTION HEARD:

2012-02-10

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO

RE:
N.H.B., Plaintiff

And

L.B., Defendant

BEFORE:
Master
Joan Haberman

COUNSEL:
Ramsey,
T. for the moving party

Shiller, B. For the responding party

REASONS FOR DECISION

Master Haberman
:

[
1
]

This is the story of the two former wives of G.B..
Each has tried to involve their children in the war they continue to wage
against one another, with extremely unfortunate results.

[
2
]

The plaintiff (“N.H.B.”) now seeks leave to
deliver a fresh as amended statement of claim, the effect of which would be to
convert her relatively straightforward defamation action into a far more
complex piece of litigation.  The action has already been set down for trial,
and a trial date was set and adjourned, so leave to bring the motion is
required and granted.

THE ORIGINAL CLAIM

[
3
]

N.H.B. is the former wife of G.B. (“B.”).  The
two were married from 1976 - 2003, and had children together.  A.B. (“A.”) is
their
son.

[
4
]

After the marriage ended, G.B. married the
defendant, L.B. (“L”) but they separated in 2007. When she met G.B., L.B.
already had a daughter from a previous relationship, L.M.C. (”L.”).

[
5
]

In the spring of 2008, L.M.C. alleged that A.B.
had sexually assaulted her years earlier.  At the time the action was commenced
(July 22, 2008), these charges were still before the court.

[
6
]

This action originally stems from comments made
by L.B. to two members of the executive of Jewish Women International Canada
(JWIC).  The first incident involves a telephone conversation with Penny
Krowitz, executive director of the organization, which took place on July 2,
2008.

[
7
]

N.H.B. alleges that L.B. called Ms. Krowitz to
inform her of the sexual assault charges pending against A.B..    It is alleged
that L.B. did this, knowing that N.H.B. was a board member of the organization
and was being treated for ovarian cancer at that time.

[
8
]

It is further alleged that, on the same day,
L.B. wrote to Jill Lieberman, the president of JWIC, stating as follows:

A.B. (son of G.B. and N.B.) has been
criminally charged with the Sexual Assault of my daughter L.M.C..  The crime
occurred on May 31st of 2003.  I walked in to (sic) L.M.C.’s room and witnessed
the despicable crime inflicted upon my 15-year old daughter...

I have been separated from G.B for over
a year, and my daughter now has the strength to proceed and has in fact laid
criminal charges for which A.B. has been arrested, fingerprinted.....

...N.B. is clearly aware of what
happened and chose to do nothing to help L.M.C. {my daughter} (sic) who is in
no way different from the women your organization helps.  I am sure you are
able to see the hypocrisy in that...

[
9
]

These allegations form the core of the action as
it currently stands.

[
10
]

The statement of claim was issued a few weeks
after these events and a statement of defence was delivered in September
2008.   In her defence, L.B. claims that A.B. repeatedly sexually assaulted
L.M.C. starting just after her 14
th
birthday, and that she caught
him “raping” her daughter on June 13, 2003 (rather than May 31
st
,
2003 as Ms. Lieberman was told).   She therefore relies on the defence of fair
comment

and denies that her actions were motivated by malice.

THE EVENTS THAT FOLLOWED

This action

[
11
]

This action proceeded with remarkable speed.  In
December, 2008, less than five months after the claim was issued, the trial
record was passed.  The matter was pre-tried in January 2010

and the
trial was scheduled to begin on May 2011.  At that time, as adjournment was
sought as N.H.B. wished to amend her pleading.

That was nine months
ago.

[
12
]

This motion to amend was initially returnable in
June 2011 but adjourned on consent to July.  In July, it was adjourned by the

court because of scheduling issues.   A new date of December 5, 2011 was
selected but the matter was again adjourned.

[
13
]

In the interim, N.H.B. launched and then
withdrew Mareva injunction proceedings against L.B..

Though costs were
awarded to L.B. at that time, Conway J. noted that she was discounting the
quantum awarded as much of the costs could have been avoided by more
cooperation on the part of defence counsel.   And so the war continued.

[
14
]

Current counsel went on the record for N.H.B. in
September 2011.  The motion to amend, however, was not heard until February 10,
2012.

The criminal proceedings against A.B.

[
15
]

A.B.’s criminal charges were dealt with before
McWatt, J. on March 24, 2011, at which time all charges were dismissed.

[
16
]

As her Honour put it:

...and I believe
at the root of all of this was
a broken relationship and money and hard feelings and here we are in a court of
law litigating over something, I believe, actually didn’t happen.

[
17
]

The judge commented on the evidence, stating
that she found it illogical.  From L.M.C.’s testimony she found that the girl
appeared to feel safe in the home and that she had not complained at all about
these alleged events. She was also struck by L.M.C.’s demeanour, which she
found mirrored her mother’s.  Both displayed a “stilted, guarded and dismissive
attitude” about what had allegedly occurred, such that the court concluded
their evidence was contrived.

[
18
]

McWatt J. also commented on inconsistencies
between L.B.’s evidence at the time disclosure was made and at trial, such that
“
her credibility is particularly problematic.”
On the other hand, she
found A.B. to have been “candid, honest, uncontrived in his evidence”.   She
therefore believed and acquitted him.

[
19
]

The Reasons were wrapped up as follows:

...in the context of the family law and civil
suits, there was a motive for the complainant to lie.  I also find that
I
can infer that she was trapped in her mother’s camp
and that the camp was
against Mr. N.B. and A.B..

[
20
]

The judge also found the case against A.B. to
have been “beyond weak”.

[
21
]

On the basis of the outcome and these Reasons,
A.B. may well have a basis to commence an action for malicious prosecution
against L.B. and L.M.C., but he does appear to be interested in pursuing the
issue.  Instead, his mother now seeks redress on the basis of an alleged
assignment by A.B. to her of his rights of action arising from the initiation
of these criminal proceedings.

THE ASSIGNMENT

[
22
]

This action was started in 2008, within weeks of
the alleged defamatory comments and it was restricted to those comments.   The
criminal trial resulting in an acquittal took place in March 2011.  The
decision to amend the claim appears to have been made in May 2011 as the court
was advised of N.H.B.’s desire to adjourn her trial in order to amend her
pleading on May 16, 2011.

[
23
]

As noted above, the motion was first scheduled
for June, then July 2011.  However, it was only on October 21, 2011 that A.B.
apparently assigned his interest in any claims he may have against L.B. arising
from his criminal prosecution to N.H.B..

[
24
]

Although this alleged assignment did not occur
until after this motion had already come before the court twice, the only
evidence filed about this unusual arrangement comes through the mouth of Alice
Tse, a legal assistant in the offices of plaintiffs’ counsel.  She says nothing
about the timing of the arrangement; how or why it came about; and what
consideration was given for it.

[
25
]

Tse is also in no position to give evidence as
to whether consideration was given for the assignment as she is not a party to
it – only A.B. or N.H.B. could have attested to that to avoid the rule against
hearsay.   At the very least, one would have expected Tse to say that she was
so advised as to the consideration given by N.H.B. and that he believes the
information to be true.  Instead, Tse fails to say how she knows about the
assignment or whether she believes that what she was presumably told or read
about it was true.  She simply states that this assignment occurred.

[
26
]

A copy of the purported assignment is attached
to Tse’s affidavit as an exhibit.  Among the recitations are the following:

AND WHEREAS N.H.B. paid for all of the
costs associated with A.B.’s defence in respect of those charges together with
additional costs incurred on behalf of A.B. related to and the result of the
criminal prosecution (together called the “Costs of the Defence”)

...In consideration of the Costs of the
Defence A. B. (the “Assignor”) does hereby make an absolute assignment.....

[
27
]

The document appears to have been signed by both
A.B. and N.H.B..  However, there is no evidence from either of them indicating
that that is, in fact, the case.  There is also no evidence that N.H.B.
actually paid anything to or on behalf of A.B.; that if she did so,
particularly in the context of the “additional costs”, whether she would have
been paying for those in any event; and whether there was any agreement or even
understanding between mother and son that N.H.B. would be looking to A.B. for
reimbursement of these costs.

[
28
]

The recitals within this document are not
evidence that the statements made within it are, in fact, true.  They must be
proven by independent evidence from at least one of the two parties to the
assignment, or, at the very least, on the basis of information and belief.
Strangely, neither N.H.B. nor A.B. has sworn an affidavit in support of the
motion and Tse does not site the source of her information.

[
29
]

In the absence of a proper evidentiary
foundation for this document, I am unable to attribute any weight to it.  This
has a considerable impact on the outcome of this motion.

THE PROPOSED NEW PLEADING

[
30
]

N.H.B. now seeks to deliver a Fresh as Amended
Statement of Claim, taking her simple defamation action consisting of 5 pages
to a 13-page action with multiple causes of action.

[
31
]

She now claims for the following in addition to
defamation:

o

Intentional infliction of mental and emotional distress;

o

Conspiracy to injure;

o

Malicious prosecution; and

o

Damages under s. 61 of the
Family Law Act

[
32
]

It is noteworthy that A.B. has not sought to
join his mother in the claim nor does N.H.B. seek to add L.M.C. as a defendant,
though she seeks redress for malicious prosecution.

[
33
]

Though the motion was returnable in June, July
and December 2011, this proposed draft pleading was only drafted in January
2012.

ANALYSIS and CONCLUSION

General comments

[
34
]

The motion is brought under Rule 26.01, a
mandatory provision (
the court shall grant leave to amend)
, such that
the court is duty bound to grant the relief sought unless to do so would cause
prejudice that cannot be compensated for by costs or an adjournment.

[
35
]

Case law has also made it clear that leave to
amend should not be granted where what is pleaded is untenable at law, such
that even if all of the facts as alleged can be proved, when taken together,
they do not make out the legal conclusion a party hopes the court to draw.

[
36
]

Accordingly, where particular torts are alleged,
the court must consider the allegations in the proposed claim in the context of
the constituent elements of that tort.  If the proposed claim falls short of
alleging the presence of all of the required elements, leave to amend cannot be
granted.

[
37
]

Rule 25.06(8) also requires that certain causes
of action must be pleaded in a more detailed manner:

Where fraud, misrepresentation, breach of trust,
malice
or intent is alleged, the pleading shall contain full particulars
, but
knowledge may be alleged as a fact without pleading the circumstances from
which it is inferred.

[
38
]

Thus, bald assertions of malice or intent will
fall below the standard that a party seeking to so plead must meet (see
AGFA
Inc. v. Partners Prepress
,
[2006] OJ No. 3373
).

[
39
]

The most appropriate way to address the proposed
draft pleading is to review each new cause of action and to assess whether it
can stand in the context of the facts that have been pleaded and the applicable
legal tests.

Intentional infliction of mental and
emotional distress

[
40
]

In this regard, N.H.B. alleges that L.B. was
aware she had been diagnosed with ovarian cancer in May 2008 and that her
actions thereafter were targeted at causing her stress.

She claims
that the defamation and malicious prosecution fractured her family and caused “stress,
discord and anxiety” among her children when she needed their comfort.

[
41
]

N.H.B. adds that L.B.’s action was calculated to
cause her “prolonged and intense mental and emotional distress”, adding that
the malicious prosecution was an additional source of mental anxiety for her
and that, instead of receiving her son’s support while she battled cancer, she
had to provide him with “extra financial and emotional support.”

[
42
]

These allegations are contained in paragraphs
34-37 of the proposed pleading and L.B. does not oppose this aspect of the
proposed claim.   They can therefore be added to the statement of claim as it
currently stands, but only insofar as they refer to infliction of mental and
emotional distress caused by the alleged defamation.  The references to
malicious prosecution must be deleted.

[
43
]

Except as expressly provided by legislation,
such as s. 61 of the
Family Law Act
, our law does not provide for recovery
for “ricochet victims” of a tort.   Thus, unless N.H.B. can bring herself
within the provisions of s. 61, she is not entitled to general damages as a
result of having suffered distress because of something that was done to her
son.

Conspiracy to injure

[
44
]

At paragraph 38 of the proposed pleading, N.H.B.
states that the acts described above (the allegations supporting the claims for
malicious prosecution and intended infliction of mental distress) constitute
the tort of conspiracy to injure.  Though L.M.C. has not been added to the
claim, N.H.B. speaks of acts committed by L.B. and L.M.C. as constituting the
conspiracy. When she speaks of motive, however, she refers to L.B., only.

[
45
]

In the context of this tort, N.H.B. claims
special damages that were sustained by A.B. along with her own general
damages.  In paragraph 38, she claims that L.B.’s motive was to cause injury to
her “by harming her son”, again an attempt to set herself up as a ricochet
victim.  In paragraph 39, N.H.B. relies on the assignment as a basis for
allowing her to claim A.B.’s special damages for conspiracy to injure along
with her own general damages.

[
46
]

L.B. is already being sued for intentional
infliction of mental and emotional distress.  It is unclear what a claim for
conspiracy adds to that. In any event, N.H.B. does not appear to have pleaded
the constituent elements of this tort.

[
47
]

The tort of conspiracy requires:

1)

two or more persons
, who either: a) use lawful or unlawful means for the
predominant
purpose of injuring the plaintiff
; or b) use unlawful means with knowledge
that that acts were aimed at the plaintiff and
knowing or constructively
knowing that they would cause injury to the plaintiff;

2)

an agreement to injure between two or more
persons
;

3)

acts in furtherance of the agreement to injure;
and

4)

damages suffered by the plaintiff as a result of
the defendants’ conduct (see
Harris v. GlaxoSmithKline Inc.
(2010),
2010 ONSC 2326 (CanLII)
, 101
OR (3d) 665);
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc
.,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 SCR, 959).

L.M.C.

[
48
]

N.H.B.’s counsel was unable to point to any case
law involving a claim for conspiracy where only one defendant has been sued.
In fact, the cases often speak of the pre-conditions in terms of “two or more
defendants”.

[
49
]

L.M.C. has not been sued as a co-conspirator.
Thus, based on the current state of the law, this, alone, appears to be a fatal
to the claim.   There is no precedent I am aware of for simply naming a
co-conspirator in the body of a claim, thereby insulating oneself from the
costs they would be entitled to claim if they had been sued and prevailed.

[
50
]

Simply naming a co-conspirator in the body of
the claim also deprives them of a voice in a proceeding that is open to the
public, such that they have no input into its resolution or its outcome.  This
is not a practice the court should endorse as it allows for a court-sanctioned
form of defamation in a pleading with no possible repercussion to the
plaintiff.

[
51
]

Further, N.H.B. has not alleged that L.M.C.
agreed with her mother to injure either N.H.B. or A.B., intentionally or even
knowingly.   This essential element of the tort is also absent.

[
52
]

Finally, the court has been left to infer malice
on the part of the co-conspirators based on A.B.’s acquittal.  While McWatt J’s
reasons will go some way to helping a civil court assess L.B.’s credibility, it
is open for a court to find that L.M.C., only 15 at the time of this alleged
assault, was her mother’s unwitting accomplice.  As her Honour put it, L.M.C.
was “trapped” in her mother’s camp.  Thus, the judge’s Reasons will certainly
not suffice to allow the court to attribute negative motives to L.M.C..   Rule
25.06(8) requires more than a few very short paragraphs before a tort of this
kind can be advanced.

[
53
]

I find that the tort of conspiracy has not been
properly pleaded as some of the essential elements of the tort are absent from
the proposed draft.  On this basis, alone, this portion of the proposed
pleading cannot stand.

A.B.

[
54
]

If my analysis is not correct, there is a
further problem with the way in which this tort has been pleaded, in terms of
N.H.B.’s attempt to seek relief for A.B.’s special damages.

[
55
]

I have already indicated that the assignment
through which N.H.B. expressly pursues this claim (paragraph 39 of the proposed
pleading) has not been properly proven.   While the factual allegations in the
pleading must be taken as capable of being proven for the purpose of the
motion, that proposition does not extend to the vehicle through which N.H.B.
advances A.B.’s claims.

[
56
]

The validity of that assignment is a
prerequisite to this manoeuvre. Thus, both the existence and legitimacy of the
assignment must be proven.  Ideally, both A.B. and N.H.B. would have provided
an affidavit, asserting that they each signed the assignment and that the
recitals in it are accurate.  At least one of them ought to have discussed the
nature and timing of the  consideration provided and explained how it is that
the motion was scheduled to be heard twice before the assignment even came into
existence.  A.B.’s evidence on these issues was critical, in view of the fact
that he appears to be walking away from his own potential claim for general
damages.

[
57
]

There is the further problem that conspiracy to
injure is a personal claim, thus not capable of being assigned.  Both the
plaintiff’s factum and oral submissions made on N.H.B.’s behalf simply washed
over these issues without actually addressing them.

[
58
]

The leading case in the area is
Frederickson
v. Insurance Corp. of British Columbia

1986 CanLII 1066 (BC CA)
, 28 DLR (4
th
) 414 (BC
Court of Appeal;
1988 CanLII 38 (SCC)
, [1988] SCJ No 54, dismissing the appeal and adopting the
reasons of McLaughlin J.).

[
59
]

There, the BC court discussed the assignability
of a cause of action in tort in the context of   damages stemming from personal
injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident.   The court began by examining
the general principle that a bare cause of action is not assignable.

[
60
]

They then reviewed the exceptions to the general
principle.  One exception where an assignment will be recognized involves an
assignee who has a pre-existing property interest or legitimate commercial
interest in the enforcement of the claim.  N.H.B. points to this exception as
the basis for suggesting that the assignment to her is valid.

[
61
]

However, when one reviews the case and considers
the policy reasons for the exception, it is clear that evidence is required to
show either that the property interest was pre-existing or that the commercial
interest is legitimate.  Thus, evidence is needed in order to show the court
that a party’s case fits within an exception to the general prohibition.  As I
have found N.H.B. failed to file any evidence to support the validity of the
assignment, I am unable to say that it fits within the exceptions to the
prohibition against assigning rights of action based in tort.

[
62
]

The court goes on in
Frederickson

to make
it clear that this exception is not universal, but rather is restricted in its
application:

An assignment were the assignee possesses such an
interest will be valid,
provided the action in tort is not based on a
personal wrong such as assault, libel or personal injury.
The reason for
the latter stricture appears to be that
in cases of personal torts, the
assigned can have no legitimate property or commercial interest
in
recovery.

[
63
]

This statement of law has been picked up by
Ontario courts (see
528650) Ontario Ltd. (c.o.b. Ontario Heater & Supply
Co.) v. Hepburn

[2003] OJ No. 2779
).  In 2011, our Court of Appeal referred
to
Frederickson
as the leading Canadian case on assignability of a cause
of action in tort.

[
64
]

N.H.B. has tried to counter these well accepted
statements of law by reference to two cases.  The first,
Willmott v. Norton

2001 BCSC 478
, deals with an assignment of an action for damages arising from
sexual assault.   The plaintiff was a student at the time, the defendant, an
instructor at the college he attended.    After the defendant pleaded guilty to
criminal charges laid as a result of the incident, the college settled directly
with the plaintiff and took an assignment of his rights to proceed against the
assailant.  In that case, the court was of the view that the assignment was
valid.

[
65
]

When one analyzes the factual matrix,
Willmott

actually appears to be a form of subrogation rather than an assignment of a
right of action.  Having compensated the plaintiff for the damages he suffered,
something the college felt duty-bound to do, they then stepped into his shoes
and went after the actual tort-feasor.

[
66
]

There are clear policy reasons for promoting
this type of arrangement, which provides a plaintiff with compensation earlier
and more easily than he might otherwise have received it, in the context where
an assailant has already pleaded guilty.   That is quite different from the
case at bar.  There is no suggestion here that N.H.B. paid her son for the
damages he sustained and that she now seeks to step into his shoes.  Instead
she seeks to recover what she paid to his counsel on his behalf and to him for
his living expenses.

[
67
]

The Alberta Court of Appeal’s decision in
Margetts
v. Timmer Estate
1999 ABCA 268 (CanLII)
, 244 AR 114,

also involves assignments of damages
claims, this time where insurers paid out plaintiffs in motor vehicle
accidents.  Having settled with the injured parties, the insurers then took
assignments of their claims in order to pursue the responsible parties.

[
68
]

Again, this is a form of subrogation, a well
recognized principle, supported by sound policy reasons.   As in
Willmott
,
it allows for early payment of compensation to injured plaintiffs, a laudable
objective.

[
69
]

In
Margetts
, the court justified its
approach by looking at general principles and the exceptions to them, driving
home the desire to prohibit intermeddling for collateral purposes.  As the
court stated:

The true question to be determined in the light of
the contents of the agreement and the entire transaction is
whether it is
for a legitimate purpose that does not jeopardize the integrity of the judicial
process.

[
70
]

In both of the cases relied on by the plaintiff,
evidence was filed discussing how the assignment came about.  This allowed the
court to consider the true question: whether the assignment was for a
legitimate purpose.  Thus, both cases are distinguishable as no such evidence
was filed here.

[
71
]

In the absence of evidence, the court must fall
back on the general principle enunciated in
Frederickson
and prohibit an
assignment of a tort based on a personal wrong.    Thus, even if the assignment
has been properly supported by evidence, it is not clear that, in light of the
current state of the law, it could achieve the effect N.H.B. desires.

[
72
]

In this case, it is certainly not clear on its
face why N.H.B., rather than A.B., is seeking damages that A.B. suffered.  Even
if N.H.B. could sue for A.B.’s special damages, why is he not pursing his
general damages?  The absence of evidence regarding the circumstances behind
this assignment raises many unanswered questions about A.B.’s role.

[
73
]

My concerns are exacerbated by the fact that the
assignment, such as it is, was not even signed until after this motion had
already come before the court.  In the face of all of this, a factual context
provided in proper evidentiary form was required to set the stage before the
document could be relied on for anything,

[
74
]

For all of the foregoing reasons, I am not
prepared to permit the amendments that pertain to the tort of conspiracy to
injure as there is no legal basis for such a claim on the facts as pleaded.

Malicious prosecution

[
75
]

Again, N.H.B. relies on the assignment from
A.B., as she seeks to advance his claim for legal and related expenses of
$150,000.  She also claims to have provided him with financial support
totalling $150,000 to replace income he might have otherwise earned.  She
claims that A.B. “was consumed with immobilizing anxiety stemming from the
criminal proceeding and he was not able to work” from their inception until his
acquittal.   Yet, A.B. does not seek general damages.

[
76
]

N.H.B. maintains that L.B. knew or ought to have
known that she would pay these expenses as she was A.B.’s sole financial
support.   This suggests that she was already supporting him at the time of
these events.  It is not clear how old A.B. was at the time of these events or
what has become of his father.

[
77
]

Again, this is a very personal form of action
that only A.B. can advance.  Even if the assignment has been properly
explained, it would not, in my view, permit an assignment of this kind of
claim, for the reasons set out above with respect to the tort of conspiracy to
injure.

[
78
]

The current composition of this action totally
ignores the reality of proceeding to discoveries and through to trial.  L.M.C.
is not a party so cannot be examined for discovery as to the liability issues –
about why she laid these charges to start with and why she persisted with her
allegations.  How will N.H.B. prove that L.M.C. lacked reasonable and probably
grounds to lay these charges, a requisite element of the tort, without having
named her as party to the action?

[
79
]

Similarly, A.B. cannot be examined regarding his
damages – can N.H.B. provide copies of all legal accounts?  Is she in a
position to speak to why A.B. was not able to work?

[
80
]

I have already indicated that A.B. would likely
be a reticent witness in view of his having opted to walk away from his
potential claim for general damages.   Similarly, after having gone through a
criminal trial for sexual assault only to have the charges dismissed, L.M.C.,
too, will likely be a reluctant witness.  This would result in a trial that
hinges entirely on the testimony of two individuals, neither of whom is a party
to the action.

[
81
]

When asked about how this would proceed to
discoveries and trial, N.H.B.’s counsel said they would rely on the transcript
from the criminal proceeding and on the acquittal.  This betrays a lack of
understanding as to how an acquittal in a criminal trial is treated by a civil
court.

[
82
]

When a party is convicted of a criminal offence
that is inextricably intertwined with a civil action, the conviction stands as
prima facie proof of guilt, and can be introduced for that purpose at trial.

[
83
]

An acquittal, however, simply means that that
the court has reasonable doubt.  In this case, McWatt J. went some way towards
making it clear that she believed A.B. and that she felt the Crown had had a
very weak case – but that does not change the fact that the burden of proof in
the civil matter is somewhat lower than that in the criminal proceeding.  The
entire panoply of issues involved in the criminal action would have to be
re-examined in the civil action.  The acquittal does not stand as prima facie
proof of anything in this law suit, where it would only be necessary to show
that A.B. did what L.M.C. accused him of doing on a balance of
probabilities.

[
84
]

The above issues - practical issues - illustrate
why the claim cannot stand as pleaded.

[
85
]

The allegations regarding malicious prosecution
must also be deleted from the proposed pleading.  This is a personal claim that
cannot be assigned and, in any event, the assignment relied on to support the
claim has not been proven.

s. 61,
Family Law Act

[
86
]

It is trite laws that the Act sets up a
derivative claim for those near and dear to parties who are injured though the
fault of others.

[
87
]

N.H.B. tries to add this as an alternative to
her claim for conspiracy to injure.  At paragraph 41 of her proposed pleading
she states that she can claim the $300,000 she paid to and on A.B.’s behalf for
his living and legal expenses under the Act.  She also claims $100,000 for her own
loss of guidance, care and companionship which she claims she “expected to
receive from A.B. while she was battling cancer.”

[
88
]

I turn to Glithero J.’s decision in
Munro v.
the Queen in Right of Canada

1992 CanLII 7423 (ON CTGD)
, [1992] OJ No. 2453 for a discussion as to the
operation of this provision.  That case, too involved a claim for malicious
prosecution.  In that case the action was brought by Munro, a former federal
cabinet minister after the charges brought against him ended in his favour.
His family members sought recompense pursuant to this provision.

[
89
]

The court struck the FLA claims, stating that
the precondition to the application of such a claim, which is derivative in
nature, is an injury – meaning
an interference with the physical or mental
integrity of the person in a medical sense
.  The types of injury associated
with a claim for malicious prosecution – such as
“injury” to the person’s
reputation, pride, community standing or economic condition
do not support
a claim under the FLA.  As the claims could not succeed, they were struck.

[
90
]

Further, s. 61 does not contemplate legal costs
as a recoverable head – these would not constitute
actual expenses
reasonably incurred for the benefit of an injured person
as they did not go
towards purchasing treatment or traveling to or from same.

[
91
]

The motion is therefore dismissed with respect
to this claim, as well.  This claim cannot be added to the pleading as it
cannot lead to a recovery.  It is untenable at law.
